docs.title: Portal SDK — Design Token Reference
docs.text: Write theme-adaptive styles without importing MUI or Backstage APIs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Portal injects CSS custom properties (design tokens) onto a display: contents wrapper around every contributed component. These tokens reflect the active Backstage theme — they update automatically when the user switches between light, dark, and high-contrast themes.

Plugin authors should use these tokens for all colour values instead of hardcoding hex values or importing MUI's useTheme().

docs.title: How tokens are injected
docs.text:
When the host renders a contributed tab or card, it wraps the component in a ContributionWrapper:

// Simplified from portal-extension-host/src/ExtensionRenderer.tsx
<ContributionWrapper>
  <ErrorBoundary>
    <YourContributedComponent />
  </ErrorBoundary>
</ContributionWrapper>

ContributionWrapper renders a div with display: contents and sets all 10 CSS custom properties from useTheme().palette. Because display: contents generates no layout box, the wrapper is invisible to flex and grid containers — it does not affect your component's layout.

docs.title: Theme-adaptive tokens
docs.text:
These 10 tokens are available in every contributed component:

CSS custom property MUI source Description --portal-color-primary palette.primary.main Brand primary (Red Hat red) --portal-color-primary-light palette.primary.light Lightened primary for hover states --portal-color-primary-dark palette.primary.dark Darkened primary for active states --portal-color-error palette.error.main Error red --portal-color-warning palette.warning.main Warning amber --portal-color-success palette.success.main Success green --portal-color-text-primary palette.text.primary Primary text — high contrast --portal-color-text-secondary palette.text.secondary Secondary text — muted --portal-color-background palette.background.default Page background --portal-color-surface palette.background.paper Card / surface background

docs.title: Using tokens in components
docs.text:
// No MUI import needed:
export function TrustSignalsCard() {
  return (
    <div
      style={{
        backgroundColor: 'var(--portal-color-surface)',
        border: '1px solid var(--portal-color-primary)',
        borderRadius: '4px',
        padding: '16px',
      }}
    >
      <h3 style={{ color: 'var(--portal-color-primary)', margin: 0 }}>
        Trust Score
      </h3>
      <p style={{ color: 'var(--portal-color-text-secondary)' }}>
        Supply chain verification status
      </p>
      <span style={{ color: 'var(--portal-color-success)' }}>✓ Verified</span>
    </div>
  );
}

docs.title: Using tokens in CSS-in-JS
docs.text:
If your plugin uses makeStyles (MUI v4), you can still reference the custom properties:

import { makeStyles } from '@material-ui/core/styles';

const useStyles = makeStyles({
  card: {
    backgroundColor: 'var(--portal-color-surface)',
    borderLeft: '4px solid var(--portal-color-primary)',
  },
  title: {
    color: 'var(--portal-color-text-primary)',
  },
  subtitle: {
    color: 'var(--portal-color-text-secondary)',
    fontSize: '0.875rem',
  },
});

docs.title: Reading tokens programmatically
docs.text:
If you need the current token values in JavaScript (e.g. for a canvas or chart library), use usePortalCssTokens from @ansible/portal-extension-host:

import { usePortalCssTokens } from '@ansible/portal-extension-host';

function MyChartComponent() {
  const tokens = usePortalCssTokens();
  // tokens['--portal-color-primary'] → '#ee0000' (example)

  return (
    <canvas
      ref={canvasRef}
      style={tokens} // spread onto any element to inherit tokens
    />
  );
}

Note: usePortalCssTokens requires @material-ui/core as a dependency. It is available from portal-extension-host, which is a host package. Plugin authors who need the values in JavaScript should add @ansible/portal-extension-host as a dependency or use getComputedStyle(element).getPropertyValue('--portal-color-primary') on a rendered DOM node.

docs.title: Theme light / dark comparison
docs.text:
Token Light theme (example) Dark theme (example) --portal-color-primary #ee0000 #ff4d4d --portal-color-background #ffffff #1b1b1b --portal-color-surface #f5f5f5 #2c2c2c --portal-color-text-primary rgba(0,0,0,0.87) rgba(255,255,255,0.87) --portal-color-text-secondary rgba(0,0,0,0.54) rgba(255,255,255,0.60)

Exact values depend on the Backstage theme configured in the host. The tokens always reflect the active theme — you do not need to implement your own dark mode toggle.

docs.title: Static tokens
docs.text:
For fixed sizing values (spacing, border radii) that do not need to adapt to the theme, @ansible/portal-plugin-sdk exports static constants:

import { PORTAL_TOKENS } from '@ansible/portal-plugin-sdk';

// Use in inline styles or makeStyles:
padding: PORTAL_TOKENS.spacing.card; // '12px'
padding: PORTAL_TOKENS.spacing.page; // '24px'
borderRadius: PORTAL_TOKENS.borderRadius.card; // '4px'

These are compile-time constants, not CSS custom properties, and do not change at runtime.

docs.title: Anti-patterns to avoid
docs.text:
❌ Don't hardcode colours:

// Wrong — breaks dark mode
<div style={{ color: '#333333' }}>

❌ Don't import MUI useTheme in contributed components:

// Wrong — creates a MUI singleton dependency in the plugin bundle
import { useTheme } from '@material-ui/core/styles';
const { palette } = useTheme();

❌ Don't use Backstage's UnifiedThemeProvider or createUnifiedTheme in plugins: Backstage's unified theme is configured by the host app. Plugins should consume the host's theme via tokens, not re-configure it.

✅ Do use CSS custom properties:

// Correct — theme-adaptive, no import needed
<div style={{ color: 'var(--portal-color-text-primary)' }}>

✅ Do use static tokens for sizing:

import { PORTAL_TOKENS } from '@ansible/portal-plugin-sdk';
<div style={{ padding: PORTAL_TOKENS.spacing.card }}>

docs.title: Adding new tokens
docs.text: If you need a colour that is not covered by the current 10 tokens, open a proposal in docs/next/ rather than hardcoding values. Token additions are non-breaking (existing consumers are unaffected) and are reviewed for naming consistency before being added to ContributionWrapper and this reference.

docs.title: Portal NFS composition
docs.text: For package/runtime Mermaid diagrams, see SDK architecture. For contributor repository structure, APIs, examples and acceptance requirements, see the third-party plugin author guide.

docs.title: Composition model
docs.text:
The host owns the entity.detail.tabs interaction and placement. Contributors declare static Blueprint extensions in their ./alpha entry points. NFS supplies typed entity, catalog, and scaffolder-field descriptors to api:portal/contributions, an app-scoped API extension owned by the portal frontend plugin. Pages share its validated snapshot through portalContributionsApiRef. There is no native global contribution registry, module-load registration, or imperative module resolver in this path.

The adapters live in @ansible/portal-extension-api/alpha and @ansible/portal-extension-host/alpha. Shared extension data references use stable IDs rather than a shared mutable singleton. Installing a plugin loads its declarations, but component loaders are deferred until filtering and authorization complete. Only the selected eligible tab loads its component.

The provider uses ApiBlueprint, avoiding an app-root wrapper that the installed Backstage API restricts to the app plugin. Scaffolder fields use the shared provider rather than attaching directly to an optional templates page. Operations remain separate from presentation and receive the current subject, not contributor-supplied URLs.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• An NFS app with a host frontend plugin whose plugin ID is portal.
  • @backstage/frontend-plugin-api 0.18.0 and compatible platform packages, matching the repository's Backstage 1.54.9 baseline.
  • A host page that resolves the current entity and canonical content type.
  • A host entitlement resolver for declared entitlement requirements.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Install createPortalContributionProvider() from @ansible/portal-extension-host/alpha once in the portal frontend plugin. The provider's extension ID is api:portal/contributions.
  2. Extend the existing host layout with useNativeEntityPage and NativeEntityActionMenu; use NativeCatalogItemActions inside an existing catalog row menu. createPortalEntityPage and createPortalCatalogPage remain reusable host factories, but installing Portal does not create a second catalog or entity UI.
  3. Render PortalEntityTabs with the descriptors and an EntityContributionContext. The host supplies the entity, canonical content type, and optional source observations. Wrap legacy component trees with compatWrapper, as demonstrated in the composition tests.
  4. Supply availableExperiences when an experience is disabled.
  5. Supply checkEntitlement from host authorization. It receives the declared entitlement and subject; the host resolves trusted organization memberships. Missing resolvers, denied decisions, and failed checks suppress entitled tabs.
  6. Install the contributor's NFS feature through app discovery or dynamic loading. Do not import its legacy index.ts for side effects.
  7. Rebuild the host and contributors together. Earlier extension declarations attached to page:portal/entity; they must use the shared provider attachment.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
From the repository root, run:

yarn test --runInBand \
  workspaces/portal-core/plugins/portal-extension-host \
  workspaces/portal-scaffolder/plugins/portal-scaffolder/src/alpha.test.tsx \
  workspaces/portal-scaffolder/plugins/portal-scaffolder/src/alphaPermissions.test.tsx \
  workspaces/apme/plugins/backstage-apme/src/alpha.test.tsx

The host tests exercise real NFS discovery, filtering, selection, permission denial, configuration and experience gates, entitlement fail-closed behavior, manifest rejection, and failure isolation. The APME test uses its actual NFS declaration and substitutes the Quality component to avoid a live backend. Shared-provider tests also cover cross-page discovery, NFS-disabled extensions, operation subjects, follow-on navigation, and refresh of already-selected results. Field composition tests cover absent and alternative templates hosts, first- and third-party fields, duplicate and malformed declarations, and preservation of field schemas and asynchronous validation. The separate scaffolder permission suite checks catalog-import denial without reusing the route-parity suite's cached permission decisions.

docs.title: Optional templates hosts
docs.text:
Portal host services and AAP authentication do not require portal-scaffolder. Application and deployment composition can omit that contributor. Install independent native plugins through their declared frontend features and normal RHDH dynamic plugin configuration; shared SDK libraries are not standalone dynamic page plugins. Existing Collections, Execution Environments, and Git repositories pages still belong to portal-scaffolder until content extraction. APME's current repository UI therefore still needs that contributor.

ScaffolderFieldBlueprint attaches declarations to api:portal/contributions through its scaffolderFields input. At app startup, the Portal provider checks actual NFS ownership, manifest references, API compatibility, content scope, field names, and duplicate names/entry-point IDs. It publishes accepted declarations as the read-only portalContributionsApiRef.scaffolderFields snapshot without invoking widget loaders.

createPortalScaffolderPage is an optional consumer adapter. When its route is opened, it supplies the shared declarations to the templates implementation. NativeScaffolderFields checks configuration, experience availability, permissions, and reserved field names before loading widgets. The returned field name must match the declaration; value/UI schemas and asynchronous validators remain part of the existing field contract.

Without a templates adapter, declarations remain discoverable but unused. No widget is loaded and no missing templates-page attachment is required. An alternative templates plugin can use the same adapter without taking the portal-scaffolder plugin ID. Field discovery does not make workflows runnable without a templates host. Application/deployment selection is separate from field discovery and does not itself extract the existing content pages. Root routing is configured separately through the Portal host's landing destination.

docs.title: Migrating field attachments
docs.text:
Prerequisites: install the shared Portal provider and build the host, templates adapter, and native contributors from a coordinated SDK revision.

  1. Keep existing ScaffolderFieldBlueprint.make descriptors, field names, manifest IDs, widget schemas, and validation functions. Rebuild the shared API and host packages, then rebuild/re-export the consuming native plugins together.
  2. Remove explicit NFS attachment overrides targeting page:portal-scaffolder/templates. The Blueprint now defaults to api:portal/contributions, input scaffolderFields. Do not restore a second page collector or legacy registration side effects.
  3. Keep createPortalScaffolderPage for the templates route. Custom composition tests must install createPortalContributionProvider() in the portal plugin, just as the real app does. The page helper retains its loader/route options; an explicit hostApiVersion adds an adapter-specific restriction to the provider's version validation.

Verify that a permitted field renders with the templates host installed and that removing that host leaves the declaration inspectable without calling its widget loader. The field tests in the repository verification command exercise both cases. Coordinated rebuilds are required; this migration does not promise mixed old/new dynamic artifact compatibility or require npm publication.

docs.title: Contribution contract
docs.text:
EntityDetailTabBlueprint.make accepts a name and a descriptor:

  • manifest: plugin metadata and capability declarations.
  • capabilityId, entryPointId: references to the capability and entity-tab entry point. Labels, order, content scope, and permission come from the entry.
  • attachment: exactly entity.detail.tabs for this contract.
  • loader: deferred component loader receiving the current subject.
  • appliesToSourceKinds: optional source constraints.
  • enabledByConfig: optional configuration key; explicit true is required.
  • requiredEntitlements: optional IDs declared in the manifest.
  • isApplicable: optional synchronous or asynchronous predicate. It narrows scope; it cannot broaden it. Exceptions suppress the tab.

The entry must have kind entity-tab, surface entity-page, and a slot launch targeting entity.detail.tabs. Its content scope must be non-empty, known, and within capability scope. Runtime predicates stay on the descriptor, not in serializable capability metadata.

The host checks ownership against the actual NFS plugin, API compatibility, references, region, content scope, and duplicate IDs. Invalid descriptors are logged and omitted without removing the rest of the page. Filtering proceeds through content/source scope, experience/configuration, permission, entitlement, and predicate before component loading. Selected components are error-bounded.

docs.title: Supported native launches
docs.text:
The internal developer-preview contract defines the author-facing boundary and proposed compatibility policy. Native launch support is limited to the following combinations:

  • Slots render through the matching declared Blueprint and its allowed host region. The host does not resolve arbitrary moduleName values.
  • Entity and catalog item actions dispatch registered operations for the current subject.
  • Entity operation actions may select an eligible detail tab after a successful response. The manifest follow-on must target entity.detail.tabs, and the descriptor must identify the matching tab with followOnEntryPointId. The destination must also pass eligibility checks. Selection does not wait for a background job to complete.
  • Catalog-header workflow actions resolve owner-prefixed workflow IDs through ScaffolderWorkflowBlueprint to template entity references, not supplied URLs.

Catalog item action follow-ons, operation-to-workflow follow-ons, arbitrary launch chains, and workflow launches on other action surfaces are unsupported. The common CapabilityLaunch union is broader than the native renderer subset; legacy launcher behavior is not the native contract.

docs.title: APME entry point
docs.text:
@ansible/plugin-backstage-apme/alpha default-exports an apme frontend plugin. It declares the Quality tab, overview summary, scan action, catalog action, and repository URL field, and registers the existing API factory through ApiBlueprint. It does not import plugin.ts or register legacy contributions.

The native declarations also cover repository Quality activity and Dependencies, catalog Quality/settings/Violations tabs, table columns, the Add repository workflow launcher, and deregistration. Scanning requires ansible.apme.enabled: true and the host-resolved apme.scanning entitlement. Configuration alone is not an entitlement decision.

The complete repository UI journey still uses portal-scaffolder's Git Repositories list/detail pages and its Templates UI for Add repository. APME has no declared package dependency on portal-scaffolder, but these presentation and navigation paths still require their current host. Its Content Quality route redirects into the repository catalog. Collecting fields independently does not extract those pages or make that full UI journey available without them.

docs.title: Acceptance boundaries
docs.text:
• The profile-only native header adapter requires a fresh packed next-2.1 acceptance run to verify that Create is absent and exactly one Sign out item completes the configured OIDC flow. Earlier header checks do not certify this revised composition. Intermittent OAuth/revocation transport errors remain separate from header wiring.
  • Earlier packed next-2.1 content checks used mock AAP authentication. The source NFS app was verified with real AAP login and two completed standalone checks on the existing my-ns-my-col test repository. Persisted scan count increased from two to four, with one finding. APME refreshes its summary while a background operation is active, then stops polling; the Portal host does not need scan-specific logic. No remediation, branch, or PR was applied.
  • The named test-amazon-aws manual entry was re-registered through the native field/workflow and deregistered through its native entity action. Catalog count changed from 123 to 124 to 123; confirmed removal redirected without a manual page reload. The existing APME project ID and zero-scan history were unchanged. These counts are test evidence, not expected deployment defaults.
  • The earlier AWS dependency-resolution failure is not evidence against native discovery, but scans of that larger repository still need their own successful assessment evidence. Do not weaken Galaxy server validation to make them pass.
  • Complete content extraction, query/write contracts, and picker migration.
  • Compatibility validation is intentionally limited to next-2.1 for this slice. The AAP resolver validates caller memberships against configured organizations. REST operations, registration adapters, and APME interactive workflows use the same resolver, independently of identity namespace. Any granted membership enables a shared capability, subject to operation and repository RBAC. Multiple memberships do not select an active organization for organization-specific handlers. Git repositories need no AAP ownership annotation or namespace mapping; new manual entries stay in default. Remaining legacy mutations and automatic scan policy are not guarantees supplied by frontend gates. See the operations backend policy.
  • The native app does not import APME's legacy entry point for registration side effects. The explicitly selected legacy fallback still has its own registration. Do not install both registration paths in the same native app.

docs.title: Loading AAP authentication in a dynamic host
docs.text:
The @ansible/aap-app-auth frontend module owns the AAP OAuth API and sign-in page. A dependency in portal-scaffolder/package.json does not install that module into an RHDH host. Each NFS deployment using AAP authentication must explicitly load its exported dynamic artifact alongside the Portal plugins.

With the exported tarball available in the host's local plugin directory, add this entry to the deployment's dynamic-plugins.yaml plugins list:

plugins:
  - package: ./local-plugins/portal/ansible-aap-app-auth-dynamic-0.1.0.tgz
    disabled: false

For a workspace-mounted development export, use the directory instead:

plugins:
  - package: ./local-plugins/portal-nfs/aap-app-auth
    disabled: false

These are alternative artifact paths, not two registrations. Adjust the path to match the deployment's exported artifact. NFS discovers the module's ./alpha entry point from its package metadata; no Scalprum signInPage or apiFactories configuration is required.

After exporting and restarting the host, verify that api:app/rhaap-auth and sign-in-page:app/rhaap are discovered. An absent AAP sign-in page or an unresolved ansible.auth.rhaap API is a reason to check the installed dynamic plugin list, not to restore authentication exports in portal-scaffolder.

docs.title: Landing behavior
docs.text:
The Portal host owns /. With no portal.landingPage override, it opens /self-service only if that NFS page is mounted. If no destination is available, Portal displays a neutral welcome message inside the existing app shell instead of redirecting to a missing page. This fallback is not a separate content catalog or a new homepage design.

An explicit override must match an installed top-level NFS page's effective path, including any NFS page-path configuration override. The host checks mounted metadata without invoking page loaders. It rejects external URLs, relative paths, /, dot segments, encoded paths, query strings, fragments, trailing slashes, and arbitrary descendants of a registered page. A missing or disabled destination also uses the fallback. An invalid explicit override does not silently select Templates or the first sidebar item.

Landing selection is not authorization: navigation enters the page through its normal NFS lifecycle, and the destination retains its permission checks. A restricted destination may show its normal access-denied state. Sidebar ordering and visibility do not grant access or change landing selection.

docs.title: Configuring the landing destination
docs.text:
Prerequisites: install the Portal native frontend host and the destination page in the NFS app. No additional landing configuration is needed for the default Templates behavior; omit portal.landingPage in the minimal configuration.

  1. To override the default, set the exact installed page path in host config:
portal:
  landingPage: /self-service/collections

This is the complete landing configuration; the field is optional. Paths are app-relative: if the app is hosted under a URL prefix, do not include that prefix or a host name in this value.

  1. Restart the source app after changing configuration. For RHDH, export/install the updated Portal artifact and restart the host with the configuration.
  2. Open the app root. Verify that it opens the selected page and that the page's normal permission checks still apply. With an unavailable destination, verify the neutral fallback rather than a missing-page redirect.

Migration: existing deployments with Templates at /self-service need no new setting. If NFS configuration moves that page, set portal.landingPage to its effective path. Deployments without portal-scaffolder may select another installed page or leave the host fallback. This does not remove portal-scaffolder from source-app or installer composition; deployment selection is separate.

Verify the routing behavior with:

yarn test --runInBand workspaces/portal-core/plugins/portal-core

The tests cover configured and default destinations, absent and disabled contributors, page-path overrides, unsafe destinations, lazy-loader isolation, and destination permission denial.

docs.title: Configuring navigation
docs.text:
Plugins own page routes and icon metadata. Portal navigation selects discovered pages; it does not install plugins or grant permissions. The self-service native pages provide the same Home, History, Build, Collections, and GitHub icons as the legacy sidebar. RBAC and Settings retain their platform plugin icons.

Enable the Portal navigation adapter by disabling the stock singleton attachment:

app:
  extensions:
    - nav-content:app/sidebar: false
    - nav-content:app/portal: true
portal:
  navigation:
    items:
      - id: templates
        path: /self-service
        title: Templates

An item selects exactly one path or NFS page extension ID. Optional title overrides its label, and placement: bottom pins it below the primary items. An expandable group instead declares a title and child links:

portal:
  navigation:
    topOffset: 64
    items:
      - id: administration
        title: Administration
        placement: bottom
        children:
          - id: rbac
            page: page:rbac
            title: RBAC
      - id: settings
        page: page:user-settings
        title: Settings
        placement: bottom

To make Administration navigate directly to RBAC, replace children with page: page:rbac. This works for any item, not only Administration. Missing plugin pages and empty groups are omitted; IDs and route targets must be unique. Group icons inherit the first available child icon; icon overrides are not a navigation config field. The paths/bottomPaths configuration remains a compatibility fallback only when items is absent. Nested item data is exposed through the host's @deepVisibility frontend schema.

The source app registers native RBAC, user settings, and Search features. Its global header reuses the existing AAP/identity logout behavior through an app-owned root wrapper. The global header has no Create button or Create-contribution API. Workflow entry points remain in the installed pages. RHDH retains its own platform header instead of loading the source app wrapper. Guest users can see navigation but remain subject to page permissions; an RBAC 403 is not a missing route.

Restart the source dev server after changing configuration or schema visibility. Re-export and restart RHDH after changing dynamic plugins. The local development guide in automation-portal-local documents workspace/packed exports, the full navigation example, cache validators, and non-destructive refresh steps.

docs.title: Profile menu contributions
docs.text:
RHDH deployments install the optional @ansible/portal-rhdh native feature alongside the platform global-header feature. The adapter only renders profile items. To remove the stock Create button and use AAP Sign out, merge these entries into the existing app.extensions list:

app:
  extensions:
    - gh-component:global-header/self-service-button: false
    - gh-menu-item:global-header/logout: false
    - app-profile-menu-item:app/aap-logout: true

The profile consumer gh-menu-item:portal-rhdh/profile is enabled by default. Enable the AAP item only when its separate auth module and backend provider are installed and configured. Otherwise keep stock logout. Preserve other auth and navigation entries. No replacement Create button is installed.

AppProfileMenuItemBlueprint contributes navigation or lazy UI-action rows to the shared provider. useNativeAppProfileMenuItems() checks user identity, declared permissions, configuration, and owned page targets. The shared SDK ProfileMenuItems renders accepted rows, closes the menu before opening a new UI surface, prevents duplicate activation while pending, and contains failures. No action implementation loads just to decide visibility. Source and RHDH consumers use the same resolver; new plugin items require no adapter edits.

The AAP auth module owns its disabled-by-default logout declaration and shared logout implementation. portal-rhdh has no AAP dependency or logout-specific extension. Enable app-profile-menu-item:app/aap-logout and keep the generic gh-menu-item:portal-rhdh/profile consumer enabled. Rebuild the provider, adapter, and AAP auth artifact together. The source NFS app explicitly installs createAapProfileModule({ logoutDisabled: false }) from aap-app-auth, without replacing its existing sign-in composition.

The AAP-owned handler clears Portal auth and redirects to AAP OIDC logout; legacy global.header/profile mount-point YAML is not its registration mechanism. This integration does not change OAuth token-exchange handling or resolve intermittent transport failures during initial sign-in.

docs.title: AAP OIDC logout
docs.text:
The existing logout component waits for identity sign-out before navigating to the AAP logout destination. This prevents the identity proxy's final redirect from overwriting the OIDC redirect. Transport failure during AAP token revocation is still reported by the auth backend; a visible logged-out browser does not prove successful server-side token revocation.

The AAP deployment must advertise /o/logout/ as its OIDC end-session endpoint. Set auth.providers.rhaap.<environment>.clientId to the public OAuth client ID. The selected environment comes from auth.environment, which defaults to development. The browser-facing AAP host comes from auth.providers.rhaap.<environment>.host, falling back to ansible.rhaap.baseUrl. Both the client ID and app.baseUrl are required whenever an AAP host resolves.

Register the serialized value of app.baseUrl (new URL(appBaseUrl).href) in the OAuth application's Post Logout Redirect URIs. For example, configuring http://localhost:3000 sends http://localhost:3000/, including the trailing slash. The registered URI must match exactly. The handler sends this serialized URL as post_logout_redirect_uri, together with the configured environment's public OAuth client ID. AAP validates the URL, presents its confirmation screen, and returns to Portal sign-in after confirmation. Cancelling leaves AAP's browser session active even though Portal auth is cleared. The public OAuth host/client ID are frontend-visible; client secrets remain backend-only. This does not bypass AAP validation or change gateway-wide settings. See logout setup and the adapter README for the configuration and verification procedure.

See the profile authoring example and RHDH adapter reference. Re-export the affected host, adapter, and contributors after shared header-contract changes. Header integration is verified on the agreed next-2.1 baseline, not every RHDH version.

Upgrade deployments that configure only ansible.rhaap.baseUrl by adding auth.providers.rhaap.<environment>.clientId and ensuring app.baseUrl is set. If a host resolves but the client ID or Portal URL is missing or invalid, logout reports "AAP browser logout is unavailable: check the OAuth client and Portal URLs" and still clears Portal auth. It does not redirect to AAP, so the AAP browser session remains active.

docs.title: Task history and RBAC
docs.text: The native frontend provides Task history at /self-service/create/tasks, with task details below that path. It has a separate navigation entry alongside the template wizard. The stock RBAC frontend is a platform plugin, not a Portal contribution; permission configuration alone does not install its UI. Native deployment must explicitly enable its package without broadening administrator identities or permission grants.

docs.title: Installed contributor has no tab
docs.text: Check api:portal/contributions, installed NFS features, current content type, configuration, experience, permission, and entitlement decisions. Inspect [Portal NFS] Rejected entity tab and [Portal NFS] Cannot activate diagnostics. Unsupported content is omitted, not shown as an error.

docs.title: Task history or RBAC is missing
docs.text: Open /self-service/create/tasks directly to distinguish missing navigation from a route or permission failure. Check page:portal-scaffolder/history and the deployed bundle. For RBAC, inspect installed dynamic packages and the existing administrator configuration; do not bypass restrictions with broader grants.

docs.title: Template field is declared but unavailable
docs.text:
Inspect the NFS extension tree for the field under api:portal/contributions, input scaffolderFields, and inspect the contribution API's validated field list in a host integration or test. A valid declaration with no templates consumer is intentionally unused; no widget import is expected.

If the field is missing from the snapshot, check native discovery, ownership, manifest/version compatibility, and duplicate IDs or field names. If it is present but an installed templates adapter does not expose it, check the configuration, experience, permission, and reserved-name gates. Loader or widget failures use the existing template-field error states. There is no separate field diagnostics page or automatic fallback registration.

docs.title: Component fails to load
docs.text: The selected tab displays a contained failure while the host page remains available. Check the contribution ID, failed chunk request, remote assets, and compatible platform versions before changing the contribution contract.

docs.title: Third-party Portal plugin author guide
docs.text:
Use the Portal contracts to contribute functionality without modifying self-service or importing another optional plugin's implementation. Declare frontend extensions statically through NFS and register backend operations through injected host services.

This guide describes the current experimental SDK for teams developing plugins inside this repository's workspaces. The preview uses workspace:^ SDK dependencies and the shared root lockfile; npm publication is not required. Supported-release compatibility guarantees and backend authorization closure are not yet complete. Use this guide for coordinated internal development, not as a production-readiness certification.

docs.title: Internal developer-preview contract
docs.text: This section defines the proposed contract for coordinated internal plugin development. The implemented behavior below is available on the SDK branch; the compatibility and migration policy still requires agreement between SDK maintainers and consuming teams. This document does not announce a published preview release or certify every existing backend path.

docs.title: Preview API boundary
docs.text:
The preview surface consists of the documented shared contracts in @ansible/portal-extension-common, native Blueprints and descriptors in @ansible/portal-extension-api/alpha, operation and entitlement clients, documented frontend SDK utilities, and injected backend services from @ansible/portal-plugin-node. Use the API entry points and native interaction contracts listed below; an exported type alone does not make every field or launch combination supported.

The host owns contribution validation, attachment regions, rendering, and navigation. Contributor packages must not import another optional plugin's implementation or take over host composition. Legacy registry helpers and module-load registration are compatibility-only, not the native authoring API. Use host-owned attachments rather than imperative moduleName resolution.

Manifests must use the actual Backstage plugin ID, owner-prefixed capability and entry-point IDs, a known experienceId, and canonical content types. Entry-point scope must not broaden capability scope. Although the shared type still contains appliesTo, native validators reject that manifest predicate; put executable predicates on frontend descriptors as isApplicable instead.

The supported launch subset is:

  • Slot contributions render through the matching native Blueprint and its allowed host attachment; a slot is not an arbitrary module or route resolver.
  • Entity actions and catalog item actions invoke registered operations using the current subject.
  • An entity operation action may follow on to an eligible entity detail tab. Declare a slot follow-on targeting entity.detail.tabs and the matching descriptor followOnEntryPointId. Navigation follows a successful operation response; it is not proof that a background job has completed.
  • Catalog-header actions start workflows mapped by ScaffolderWorkflowBlueprint to registered scaffolder template references. They do not accept arbitrary workflow URLs.

Catalog item action follow-ons, operation-to-workflow follow-ons, arbitrary multi-step launch chains, and workflow launches on other action surfaces are outside this preview subset. A CapabilityLaunch union member is not a promise that a host renderer supports it on every surface.

docs.title: Backend guarantees and author responsibilities
docs.text:
The operation dispatcher requires an authenticated user, trusted organization context, a registered owner-prefixed operation ID, a permission, and REST exposure. It checks RBAC, validates supplied input schemas, and enforces every declared requiredEntitlements requirement before calling the handler. It validates supplied output schemas after the handler returns. Schemas remain optional in the current TypeScript descriptor; preview authors should define input/output schemas for their public operation contracts.

The handler must independently authorize the subject resource, verify its supported content type, and scope domain data appropriately. Frontend filtering does not provide backend resource authorization. A deployment administrator configures entitlement grants; plugin authors declare requirements and register their definitions.

For shared resources, any trusted configured membership with the required grant can enable the capability, subject to operation and resource RBAC. Git repositories do not acquire AAP organization ownership. Organization-specific operations require one validated organization; multiple memberships do not implicitly select the first organization. There is no SDK organization selector.

The following are not dispatcher guarantees:

  • idempotent metadata does not deduplicate requests, provide an idempotency key, or make retries safe. An output validation failure does not roll back effects already performed by the handler.
  • auditCategory metadata does not select a durable audit destination. Current operation auditing emits structured logs, not a durable audit store.
  • exposure.mcp does not automatically install an MCP adapter or publish tools.
  • A successful response does not provide generic job execution, cancellation, progress storage, or background authorization revalidation. Plugins must define acceptance/progress/completion semantics for long-running work.
  • Native enablement and interactive authorization do not secure every legacy mutation or automatic scheduler path. Do not copy those paths as the model for a new plugin.

docs.title: Proposed compatibility and migration policy
docs.text:
The initial host contract is 0.1.0; coordinate compatible SDK packages and contributors as one preview baseline. This is not a requirement that every domain operation use the same version. OperationDescriptor.version records the operation contract; it does not implement version negotiation or dispatch multiple versions of the same operation ID.

The implemented manifest validator requires matching major and minor API versions before 1.0.0 and checks minimumHostApiVersion. The proposed release policy keeps 0.1.x changes compatible with the documented preview subset and uses a new minor version for incompatible changes. Package publication and release automation for that policy are not established by this document.

Before a breaking preview update, SDK maintainers and affected consuming teams should agree on the replacement API, migration instructions, required package and artifact rebuilds, and acceptance checks. Record the change in the changelog and affected author references. Do not silently remove a contract or promise an unimplemented compatibility window.

The verified development deployment baseline is RHDH next-2.1 with this branch's platform dependencies, not a supported release matrix. The image tag can change; record the tested image digest, SDK revision, package versions, and dynamic artifacts for a reproducible acceptance run. Validation beyond this baseline is not required for the current preview scope.

The shared SDK packages remain private workspace packages. Preview teams develop their plugins in this monorepo using workspace:^ dependencies, the shared root lockfile, and repository build/test tooling. Acceptance starts from a fresh clone and includes dynamic export and installation in RHDH. Public npm packages, an external repository starter, and out-of-tree onboarding are outside this preview scope, not release prerequisites. A third-party plugin is architecturally independent of the host even when its source lives in the same repository.

docs.title: Contribution and experience model
docs.text:
A host experience represents a user goal, such as Content Quality. A plugin provides capabilities that help with that goal. One capability can have a card, tab, and action while reusing one backend operation.

Choose a Blueprint by the interaction, then declare applicability. Do not create a Blueprint per plugin or content type. Host layout, permissions and lifecycle are not plugin-owned DOM hooks.

The implemented manifest requires a known experienceId; this differs from the proposed advisory recommendedExperienceId model. Do not invent experiences or assume installing a plugin creates one.

docs.title: Repository structure
docs.text:
Inside this repository, packages belong to the root Yarn workspace configuration and lockfile. The four ownership groups are portal-core, self-service, aap, and apme. They are not independent Yarn projects with separate lockfiles.

An illustrative contributor layout is:

workspaces/<contributor>/
└── plugins/
    ├── <plugin>-common/
    │   └── src/                 Shared domain types and operation descriptors
    ├── <frontend-plugin>/
    │   ├── src/alpha.tsx        Static native extension declarations
    │   ├── src/manifest.ts      Serializable capability metadata
    │   ├── src/components/     Domain UI
    │   ├── config.d.ts         Configuration schema and visibility
    │   └── package.json        Role, exports, dependencies, export script
    └── <backend-plugin-or-module>/
        ├── src/                Operation registration and domain handlers
        ├── config.d.ts
        └── package.json

A frontend-only contribution does not require a backend. A shared domain package is useful when frontend and backend consume the same contracts. A scaffolder action can live in a separate backend module, as APME demonstrates.

Create preview plugins under the appropriate workspaces/<contributor>/plugins/ ownership group and declare SDK dependencies with workspace:^. A new ownership group also requires root workspace/CI registration rather than only creating a directory. Repository co-location does not permit imports of host internals or another optional plugin's implementation. Out-of-tree development would require a separately agreed dependency delivery model and is not part of this preview.

docs.title: API entry points
docs.text:
Import or service Consumer Responsibility @ansible/portal-extension-common Frontend and backend Manifest, capability, launch, operation and subject contracts @ansible/portal-extension-api/alpha Contributor frontend Native Blueprints and typed NFS descriptor/data-reference contracts portalOperationsApiRef from @ansible/portal-extension-api Contributor frontend Execute a registered operation with subject and input portalEntitlementsApiRef from @ansible/portal-extension-api Host/frontend integration Request host-resolved entitlement decisions @ansible/portal-plugin-sdk Contributor frontend Shared UI, tokens, notifications, caching and utilities portalOperationsServiceRef from @ansible/portal-plugin-node Contributor backend Register and execute operation handlers portalHealthServiceRef from @ansible/portal-plugin-node Contributor backend Report health to the host registry portalActiveOrganizationServiceRef and portalEntitlementsServiceRef from @ansible/portal-plugin-node Backend integration Resolve trusted organization memberships and entitlement decisions @ansible/portal-extension-host/alpha Host pages/composition Install provider and native rendering adapters

The host owns portalContributionsApiRef, validation, filtering and rendering. Contributor declaration code normally uses the API library, not host rendering internals. Host integration dependencies in contributor tests do not make the contributor responsible for installing the provider.

docs.title: Supported native interaction contracts
docs.text:
Blueprint Current purpose Attachment or integration EntityDetailTabBlueprint Durable entity facet entity.detail.tabs EntityOverviewCardBlueprint Compact entity summary entity.overview.main or entity.overview.secondary EntityActionBlueprint Operation on the current entity entity.actions CatalogItemActionBlueprint Operation from a catalog item catalog.item.actions CatalogTabBlueprint Additional catalog view catalog.tabs CatalogTableColumnBlueprint Comparable catalog value catalog.table.columns CatalogHeaderActionBlueprint Catalog-level workflow entry catalog.header.actions with registered workflow ScaffolderWorkflowBlueprint Workflow/template mapping Namespaced workflow ID and template reference ScaffolderFieldBlueprint Typed custom template input scaffolder.fields via shared provider and optional templates adapter AppProfileMenuItemBlueprint Profile navigation or lazy UI action appProfileMenuItems via shared provider; source header consumer

For exact descriptor fields, use the exported types and the NFS composition guide. A union member in common types is not proof that every launch/surface combination has a renderer. Native entity actions currently dispatch operations; supported follow-ons select an eligible entity detail tab. Catalog-header workflows map to registered scaffolder templates, not arbitrary routes.

docs.title: Field declarations and optional templates adapters
docs.text:
Declare native fields through ScaffolderFieldBlueprint using the existing ScaffolderFieldDescriptor and defineScaffolderField contracts. The Blueprint attaches metadata to Portal's shared contribution provider, not to a portal-scaffolder page. The provider validates ownership, manifests, version compatibility, and duplicate IDs/names without loading the widget.

An installed templates host uses createPortalScaffolderPage and NativeScaffolderFields from @ansible/portal-extension-host/alpha to consume accepted declarations and apply runtime gates before loading widgets. Field names, value/UI schemas, component props, and validation functions are unchanged. Without a templates consumer, declarations remain inspectable but unused and widget loaders do not run. Declaring a field does not install a templates page or make its workflow available.

Contributor code does not import the optional portal-scaffolder implementation or choose its page ID. Rebuild/re-export the host and contributors together, remove old templates-page attachment overrides, and follow the field attachment migration. No imperative module resolution, global registration fallback, or npm publication is required.

docs.title: Declaring a profile menu item
docs.text: Use AppProfileMenuItemBlueprint for a profile-menu row. No change to portal-rhdh is needed for each contributor. The source header and optional RHDH adapter render the same validated declarations; plugins do not import platform header code or provide their own menu DOM.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Portal contribution provider and a profile-menu consumer are installed.
  • Your plugin has an agreed ID and any permission is defined in shared contracts and registered by its backend.
  • Navigation targets are enabled pages owned by your plugin. A UI action has the APIs or app-root UI integration it needs; the SDK does not install a dialog service merely because an action is declared.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Add a navigation declaration to your native plugin's extensions. This example assumes your plugin already registers page:content-authoring/editor through PageBlueprint:
import { AppProfileMenuItemBlueprint } from '@ansible/portal-extension-api/alpha';
import { authoringViewPermission } from './permissions';

const profileLink = AppProfileMenuItemBlueprint.make({
  name: 'authoring',
  params: {
    type: 'navigation',
    title: 'Content authoring',
    targetPage: 'page:content-authoring/editor',
    authorization: {
      type: 'permission',
      requirement: authoringViewPermission,
    },
    order: 100,
  },
});
  1. For a UI interaction instead, declare a lazy handler. For example, display a notification without accessing backend data:
const profileAction = AppProfileMenuItemBlueprint.make({
  name: 'authoring-help',
  params: {
    type: 'action',
    title: 'Authoring help',
    authorization: { type: 'authenticated' },
    order: 200,
    enabledByConfig: 'ansible.content-authoring.enabled',
    loadAction: async () => {
      const { alertApiRef } = await import('@backstage/core-plugin-api');
      return ({ apis }) => {
        const alerts = apis.get(alertApiRef);
        if (!alerts) throw new Error('Notification API is unavailable');
        alerts.post({
          message: 'Open Content authoring to create content.',
        });
      };
    },
  },
});

Include both declarations in your content-authoring plugin's extensions array alongside the editor page. A declared config gate must be frontend-visible in your plugin schema. Only UI code belongs in the handler; use registered operations for backend mutations and retain resource authorization in backend handlers. Hooks cannot run inside this callback: use the supplied API holder to access your plugin's UI service when opening a dialog.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Verify the owned navigation path, including page-path overrides, and confirm action code does not load until clicked. Test missing identity, permission denial/errors, disabled configuration/extensions, invalid destinations, action load/rejection, and a healthy sibling item. A pending action prevents repeated clicks; failure reports a recoverable host error. order applies within the Portal profile block, not unrelated platform entries.

authorization.type: 'authenticated' is for signed-in UI interactions, not a backend permission grant. The host always requires a resolved user identity. No arbitrary external navigation URL or unauthenticated action is supported. AAP logout is one opt-in contribution owned by the AAP auth module; its special session handling does not belong in the generic adapter.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A host app with the Portal contribution provider installed.
  • Compatible Portal packages and the branch's platform dependency set. The current frontend declarations use @backstage/frontend-plugin-api 0.18.0 on the Backstage 1.54.9 baseline.
  • An entity detail page supplying canonical content type and entity context.
  • An agreed plugin ID, host experience, and configuration key.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Create a serializable manifest. This minimal example displays existing subject metadata and declares no backend operation or entitlement:
// src/manifest.ts
import type { PluginManifest } from '@ansible/portal-extension-common';

export const manifest: PluginManifest = {
  id: 'quality-insights',
  version: '0.1.0',
  apiVersion: '0.1.0',
  entitlements: [],
  capabilities: [
    {
      id: 'quality-insights.subject',
      ownerPlugin: 'quality-insights',
      experienceId: 'content-quality-assessment',
      displayName: 'Subject details',
      description: 'Show the selected repository identity.',
      appliesToContentTypes: ['playbook-repository'],
      minimumHostApiVersion: '0.1.0',
      entryPoints: [
        {
          id: 'quality-insights.subject.tab',
          kind: 'entity-tab',
          surface: 'entity-page',
          label: 'Subject details',
          appliesToContentTypes: ['playbook-repository'],
          launches: { type: 'slot', targetSlot: 'entity.detail.tabs' },
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
};
  1. Declare a static extension. Use a matching NFS plugin ID, manifest references, host attachment, and configuration gate:
// src/alpha.tsx
import { createFrontendPlugin } from '@backstage/frontend-plugin-api';
import { EntityDetailTabBlueprint } from '@ansible/portal-extension-api/alpha';
import { manifest } from './manifest';

export default createFrontendPlugin({
  pluginId: 'quality-insights',
  extensions: [
    EntityDetailTabBlueprint.make({
      name: 'subject',
      params: {
        manifest,
        capabilityId: 'quality-insights.subject',
        entryPointId: 'quality-insights.subject.tab',
        attachment: 'entity.detail.tabs',
        enabledByConfig: 'ansible.quality-insights.enabled',
        loader: async ({ entity }) => {
          const { SubjectTab } = await import('./components/SubjectTab');
          return <SubjectTab name={entity.metadata.name} />;
        },
      },
    }),
  ],
});

// src/components/SubjectTab.tsx
export function SubjectTab({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return <p>Selected repository: {name}</p>;
}

  1. Export ./alpha from the frontend package, declare its backstage.role: frontend-plugin, and use compatible peer/build dependencies. Follow APME's checked-in package.json for this branch's packaging pattern. Do not register native contributions through legacy index.ts side effects.

  2. Install the frontend feature through the app composition root or dynamic package discovery. The consuming host plugin must not import the contributor implementation. Set the minimal runtime configuration:

ansible:
  quality-insights:
    enabled: true

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Open an eligible repository and select Subject details. Disable the config key and confirm the contribution disappears. Confirm it does not load on an execution-environment page. Add integration tests for invalid manifests, permission/entitlement denial where declared, and contained loader failures.

This sample demonstrates declaration shape, not a complete workspace plugin. Sensitive domain data requires explicit permission and resource checks; the sample only displays metadata already supplied by the host page.

docs.title: Adding a backend operation
docs.text:
Keep the operation descriptor in a shared domain package when both sides need it. Use an owner-prefixed ID such as quality-insights.assessment.start, an operation permission, input/output schemas, and appropriate exposure flags. The current dispatcher requires a permission and REST exposure for execution.

Declare requiredEntitlements on the backend operation descriptor when the operation depends on an entitlement. The dispatcher enforces every listed ID before invoking the handler; a frontend declaration alone does not secure it. Register the matching entitlement definitions through the injected portalEntitlementsServiceRef. Missing definitions, absent grants, denied permissions, unresolved organization, and inconsistent context deny execution.

Inject portalOperationsServiceRef into the backend feature and call operations.register({ pluginId, descriptor, handler }) during initialization. The handler receives OperationRequest and authenticated OperationContext. Validate subject access and supported resource type before domain effects.

Frontend calls use this shape:

await operationsApi.execute('quality-insights.assessment.start', {
  subject: { entityRef: 'component:default/example-repository' },
  input: {},
});

Here operationsApi is the injected portalOperationsApiRef client. Pass the host's actual current entity reference, not an arbitrary project ID or URL. The transport returns { result }; long-running work should return status/job information that the contributor can monitor without blocking the host page.

Use APME's catalog-backend-module-apme/src/operations.ts as a concrete reference for registration and resource checks, not as a claim that all backend hardening is finished. Its scan operation and interactive workflow routes enforce the trusted organization, scan entitlement, and repository access. Registration and deregistration do not require the scanning entitlement. Other legacy routes and automatic background scans still need their own policy migration.

Use resolvePortalContext({ credentials, userInfo, organizations }) when adapting another authenticated transport. Inject portalActiveOrganizationServiceRef; do not infer organization from the user namespace, SCM owner, submitted metadata, or a request header. The AAP adapter verifies current direct/team memberships against configured organizations. Resource handlers must still check catalog read permission, supported content type, and domain-specific access.

Choose the backend operation scope explicitly:

  • Omit organizationScope, or use 'organization', for organization-specific state. The dispatcher requires a single validated organizationId; multiple memberships are not an instruction to select the first. Scope persistence queries to that validated organization.
  • Use organizationScope: 'shared' for operations on shared resources such as Git repositories. Any trusted membership with the required entitlement enables availability, but operation and resource RBAC still apply. The repository does not acquire an AAP organization owner.

For example, an operation descriptor for shared repository assessment includes:

import type { OperationDescriptor } from '@ansible/portal-extension-common';
import { createPermission } from '@backstage/plugin-permission-common';

export const startAssessment: OperationDescriptor = {
  id: 'quality-insights.assessment.start',
  version: '1.0.0',
  organizationScope: 'shared',
  requiredEntitlements: ['quality-insights.assessment'],
  permission: createPermission({
    name: 'quality-insights.assessment.start',
    attributes: { action: 'create' },
  }),
  exposure: { rest: true },
  inputSchema: { type: 'object', additionalProperties: false },
};

Backend context supplies organizationId for a single membership or organizationIds for multiple memberships. There is no organization selector in this SDK flow. For display, usePortalContext reads authenticated GET /api/portal-operations/context; its result is not backend authority.

docs.title: Configuration and packaging responsibilities
docs.text:
Separate package installation, native extension configuration, capability enablement, and authorization. Loading a package does not grant permission.

For new contributions, use ansible.<capability>.enabled and a shared config reader across all capability artifacts. An absent enablement gate should disable the capability. The implementation still has legacy/backend configuration paths requiring conformance work; do not assume a native gate disables every backend route.

For an AAP deployment, a minimal entitlement policy is:

portal:
  entitlements:
    grants:
      - id: quality-insights.assessment
        organizations: [engineering]

This assumes Engineering is configured in the existing AAP provider and the capability declares the matching entitlement. An expanded multi-organization example is:

ansible:
  quality-insights:
    enabled: true
catalog:
  providers:
    rhaap:
      development:
        orgs: [Engineering, Finance]
        multiOrgEnabled: true
portal:
  entitlements:
    grants:
      - id: quality-insights.assessment
        organizations: [engineering, finance]

This expanded example is not required by the minimal tab above. It requires a matching manifest entitlement definition and descriptor requiredEntitlements: ['quality-insights.assessment']. Grants choose availability for an organization; they are not user membership proof or replacements for RBAC. Use the AAP adapter's canonical lowercase organization names in grants. organizations: ['*'] grants availability across the caller's configured memberships, not membership in every AAP organization. Deployment administrators configure grants; plugin authors declare entitlement requirements.

Shared Git repositories remain in the catalog independently of these grants. No catalog namespace mapping or ansible.io/portal-organization annotation is required. Existing records are not renamed. See the operations backend reference for the generic single-organization fallback and identity compatibility details.

Use the repository's export-dynamic scripts and actual rhdh-cli embedding options, rather than the historical Janus/Scalprum examples. Re-export consumers when shared contracts change. Packaging compatibility has only been exercised against next-2.1 in this work; supported version policy remains to be agreed. Build SDK dependencies from the same repository revision and export the resulting dynamic plugin artifacts for RHDH. This does not require npm publication, a shared mutable registry singleton, or mount-point YAML.

docs.title: Author acceptance checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] SDK and consuming-team reviewers agree on the preview subset and migration policy.
  • [ ] The SDK revision, package versions, tested RHDH image digest, and dynamic artifacts are recorded.
  • [ ] Static ./alpha declarations match the manifest and actual plugin owner.
  • [ ] IDs, host API version, known experience, content scope and attachments are valid.
  • [ ] Entry-point scope does not broaden capability scope.
  • [ ] Predicates are executable frontend descriptors, not new serialized fields.
  • [ ] Optional experiences and unsupported entities do not produce broken shells.
  • [ ] Loading, empty, failure and restricted states are defined.
  • [ ] New mutations use registered operations with permission and schema checks.
  • [ ] Backend handlers authorize the selected resource independently of the UI.
  • [ ] Backend operation entitlements are declared and registered, with denied-path tests.
  • [ ] Operation scope distinguishes shared resources from organization-specific state and uses trusted memberships.
  • [ ] Long-running operations distinguish acceptance, progress and completion.
  • [ ] Disabled configuration and missing artifacts remove the intended capability.
  • [ ] Other optional plugin implementations and private RHDH APIs are not dependencies.
  • [ ] Health uses injected host services; audit/idempotency guarantees are stated honestly.
  • [ ] Dynamic exports and the agreed platform version are verified.
  • [ ] Tests cover enabled/disabled, matching/nonmatching, denied and failure cases.

docs.title: Preview onboarding acceptance
docs.text:
Before declaring the in-repository preview ready for a consuming team, SDK maintainers and that team must complete the following from a fresh clone:

  1. Check out the agreed SDK revision, install dependencies from the repository root with ./install-deps, and confirm the team's plugin is included in root workspace/CI configuration. Keep SDK dependencies as workspace:^ and use the shared root lockfile; no separately published SDK packages are required.
  2. Run the repository checks below, build the required SDK and plugin packages, and export the plugin dynamically. Install it on the recorded RHDH baseline without importing its implementation into the host plugin.
  3. Verify a supported contribution and operation, including nonmatching content, disabled configuration, permission/entitlement denial, and contained failures.
  4. Record the results and resolve or explicitly exclude required unsupported behavior before the consuming team depends on it.

APME provides an in-tree integration reference. Each consuming team's plugin still needs fresh-clone acceptance; success in an existing developer checkout does not prove reproducibility. The checklist does not require npm publication or an external-plugin repository and does not claim this acceptance is complete.

docs.title: Repository checks
docs.text:
From the root, run the repository's normal checks:

yarn tsc
yarn lint:all
yarn test

For focused native integration tests, use the yarn test --runInBand ... command in the NFS composition guide.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Installed plugin has no contribution: check native feature discovery, api:portal/contributions, manifest references, current subject scope, configuration, experience, permissions and entitlements. Inspect host rejection diagnostics before changing the loader.

Action is visible but execution fails: inspect registered operation ID, REST exposure, schemas, caller permission, handler resource checks and current organization behavior. Do not weaken authorization to bypass a denied decision.

Changes do not appear in RHDH: rebuild/re-export the affected consumers and follow the local deployment cache/restart procedure. Source app success does not prove a packed dynamic artifact was rebuilt.

docs.title: Portal SDK — Developer Quickstart
docs.text:
Legacy compatibility example: The registration helpers below describe the legacy registry path, not the default NFS integration. For native declarations and current contribution contracts, use Portal NFS composition.

Build your first portal plugin in 30 minutes.

This guide walks you through creating a frontend plugin that contributes a custom tab to the Git Repository detail page, backed by a Node.js backend plugin that reports health and emits audit events.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Familiarity with Backstage plugin development
  • Node.js 20 or 22
  • Yarn 4 (corepack enable && corepack prepare yarn@4.9.2 --activate)
  • A running Backstage instance (or this monorepo's dev server: yarn start)

docs.title: 1. Understand the plugin model
docs.text:
A portal plugin consists of up to three parts:

my-plugin/
├── plugins/my-plugin/          # Frontend — React components, contribution registration
├── plugins/my-plugin-backend/  # Backend — Express routes, health, audit events
└── plugins/my-plugin-common/   # Optional — shared types

The frontend plugin registers contributions with the host at load time. The host renders those contributions inside experience slots with error isolation and theme injection.

The key packages:

Package Your plugin depends on it for @ansible/portal-extension-api Registering tabs, cards, manifests @ansible/portal-plugin-sdk Shared UI components, usePortalContext, useIsSuperuser @ansible/portal-plugin-node Identity middleware, health, audit events @ansible/portal-extension-host (Host only) Rendering contributions — you don't depend on this

docs.title: 2a. Package setup
docs.text:
In workspaces/my-plugin/plugins/my-plugin/package.json:

{
  "name": "@ansible/my-plugin",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "backstage": { "role": "frontend-plugin" },
  "peerDependencies": {
    "react": "^18.3.0",
    "@material-ui/core": "^4.0.0",

// src/components/TrustSignalsTab/TrustSignalsTab.tsx
import React from 'react';
import { usePortalContext } from '@ansible/portal-plugin-sdk';
import { SkeletonLoader, EmptyState } from '@ansible/portal-plugin-sdk';
import type { ActionContext } from '@ansible/portal-extension-api';

// This component receives the catalog entity for the current detail page.
export function TrustSignalsTab({ entity }: ActionContext) {
  const { organizationIds, loading, error } = usePortalContext();

  if (loading) return <SkeletonLoader count={3} />;
  if (error) return <p>Organization context is unavailable.</p>;

  // Use CSS custom properties injected by ContributionWrapper (no MUI import needed):
  return (
    <div style={{ padding: '16px' }}>
      <h3 style={{ color: 'var(--portal-color-primary)' }}>
        Trust Signals for {entity.metadata.name}
      </h3>
      <p style={{ color: 'var(--portal-color-text-secondary)' }}>
        Organizations: {organizationIds.join(', ')}
      </p>
      {/* your content */}
    </div>
  );
}

docs.title: 2d. Register in the dynamic entry point
docs.text:
// src/dynamic/index.ts
import {
  registerManifest,
  registerGitRepoDetailTab,
} from '@ansible/portal-extension-api';
import { myPluginManifest } from '../manifest';
import { TrustSignalsTab } from '../components/TrustSignalsTab';

// Register the manifest (validated by the host at startup)
registerManifest(myPluginManifest);

// Register the tab contribution
registerGitRepoDetailTab({
  id: 'my-plugin.trust-signals',
  label: 'Trust Signals',
  component: TrustSignalsTab,
});

Why two calls? The manifest describes the plugin's capabilities in a serializable format (used for validation, permission checks, and future features like feature flags). The registerGitRepoDetailTab call registers the actual React component. Both are needed.

// src/portalPlugin.ts

docs.title: 3c. Create the router
docs.text:
// src/router.ts
import Router from 'express-promise-router';
import type {
  HttpAuthService,
  UserInfoService,
  LoggerService,
} from '@backstage/backend-plugin-api';
import { portalPlugin } from './portalPlugin';
import type { ActiveOrganizationResolver } from '@ansible/portal-plugin-node';

export function createRouter(options: {
  httpAuth: HttpAuthService;
  userInfo: UserInfoService;
  logger: LoggerService;
  organizations: ActiveOrganizationResolver;
}): import('express').Router {
  const router = Router();

  // Attach req.portalContext to every authenticated request
  router.use(portalPlugin.createMiddleware(options));

  router.get('/trust-signals/:repoId', async (req, res) => {
    const { repoId } = req.params;
    const context = req.portalContext;
    if (!context) {
      res
        .status(401)
        .json({ error: 'Authenticated Portal context is required' });
      return;
    }
    const { organizationId } = context;
    if (!organizationId) {
      res
        .status(403)
        .json({ error: 'A single validated organization is required' });
      return;
    }

    // Apply resource RBAC before reading organization-specific plugin state.
    // fetchTrustSignals is your domain implementation, not an SDK export.
    const signals = await fetchTrustSignals({ organizationId, repoId });

    portalPlugin.emitAuditEvent({
      operationId: 'my-plugin.trust-signals.read',
      userId: context.userId,
      organizationId,
      outcome: 'SUCCESS',
    });

    res.json(signals);
  });

  return router;
}

docs.title: 3d. Create the Backstage backend plugin
docs.text:
// src/plugin.ts
import {
  createBackendPlugin,
  coreServices,
} from '@backstage/backend-plugin-api';
import { createRouter } from './router';
import { portalPlugin } from './portalPlugin';
import { portalActiveOrganizationServiceRef } from '@ansible/portal-plugin-node';

export const myBackendPlugin = createBackendPlugin({
  pluginId: 'my-plugin',
  register(reg) {
    reg.registerInit({
      deps: {
        logger: coreServices.logger,
        httpAuth: coreServices.httpAuth,
        userInfo: coreServices.userInfo,
        httpRouter: coreServices.httpRouter,
        organizations: portalActiveOrganizationServiceRef,
      },
      async init({ logger, httpAuth, userInfo, httpRouter, organizations }) {
        // Report unknown while initializing
        portalPlugin.pushHealthStatus({
          state: 'UNKNOWN',
          message: 'Initializing...',
        });

        const router = createRouter({
          httpAuth,
          userInfo,
          logger,
          organizations,
        });
        httpRouter.use(router);

        // Signal ready after initialization is complete
        portalPlugin.pushHealthStatus({
          state: 'READY',
          message: 'Plugin healthy.',
        });
      },
    });
  },
});
